properties.title: Automatic Patient-Specific Microwave Ablation Planning Accelerated by a Physics-Guided Deep Learning Model

properties.name: Physics-guided final-ablation surrogate and GA planner
properties.membership: Static action-conditioned surrogate/planning component; not a recurrent world model
properties.architecture: CNN encodes tumor/vessel masks; treatment embeddings affine-modulate four decoder stages; sigmoid final necrosis mask feeds constrained GA. The FEM/FDM/Arrhenius teacher evolves physics, but deployed neural surrogate maps initial geometry plus treatment duration directly to final region.

properties.design: 36/12/12 patient CT train/validation/test split, simulated endpoint labels; 13 held-out anatomy planning cases; two-specialist plan-feasibility ratings.

properties.task: Rate antenna trajectories and power/time plans for 13 anatomical cases; not prospective patient treatment
properties.outcomes: Trajectory ratings optimal/acceptable; one time/power plan indeterminate

assertions.rationale: CNN maps static tumor/vessel volumes into decoder features.
Image-derived geometry and parameter embeddings interact through affine modulation.
Upsampling decoder emits final binary ablation region; this is an endpoint component, not temporal dynamics.
Antenna geometry, power and duration are settable independent treatment inputs.
Six-dimensional antenna position/direction and power 45–100 W, duration 60–300 s define input conditions.
Treatment duration in seconds conditions a fixed single-session query.
Hard tumor coverage and OAR collision constraints plus soft normal-tissue/angle/length penalties.
Predicted endpoint masks enter GA fitness.
Operational GA produces compared plans; component planning does not establish core-WM L4.
Fixed surrogate is separate from weighted coverage/normal-tissue/trajectory objective.
Hard planning constraints disallow collision and incomplete tumor coverage in computational search, not a tested clinical fail-safe.
Same-case optimized and clinician plans are compared using predicted ablation outcomes.

Plan objective measures compare GA versus clinician-defined candidate plans on13 anatomies. Evaluation is reported; this annotation does not establish a formal categorical acceptance outcome, so no pass/fail result is inferred.

Two real specialists rate the plans; this is expert feasibility only. Evaluation is reported; this annotation does not establish a formal categorical acceptance outcome, so no pass/fail result is inferred.

Inference and end-to-end planning measured with hardware and units; numerical fullplanning time extrapolated. Evaluation is reported; this annotation does not establish a formal categorical acceptance outcome, so no pass/fail result is inferred.
The complete neural architecture maps fixed inputs to a final endpoint without a carried recurrent patient state.
Final ablation map is predicted directly; no learned successor-state update is reported in the neural model. Physics teacher time integration is separate.

assertions.applicability_reason: Learning concerns a static surrogate; no learned state-transition dependency exists for this scoped component.

assertions.rationale: Plans are optimized and evaluated with the same surrogate; independent optimized-plan mismatch stress test is not supplied.
Patient CT datasets are partitioned 36/12/12; full availability/site leakage audit not specified.
criteria_missing: Availability/site audit and complete preprocessing fit provenance

assertions.rationale: Specific code repository is explicitly said available; access not independently checked.

evidence_fragments.content:
The tumor-vessel volume was processed by a CNN-based encoder. The en-
coder repeatedly applies 3D CNN layers, instance normalization, and GELU
activation to extract high-dimensional features while reducing the spatial reso-
lution. The antenna position, antenna direction, power, and treatment duration
were separately passed through positional encoding and linear layers to generate
the affine parameters required at each decoder stage, namely the scale parameter
γand shift parameterβ.
The extracted features and affine parameters were jointly used in the decoder
blocks, allowing the feature maps to be modulated according to the treatment
conditions. Each decoder block consists of one upsampling operation and three
affine stages. In each affine stage, after a CNN layer, feature modulation was
performed by applyingγandβto the feature mapXasX ′ =X·γ+β[18]. The
spatial resolution was progressively restored through four decoder blocks, and
encoder features were combined with decoder features through skip connections
using channel-wise concatenation.
Finally, the output was passed through a sigmoid function to obtain a prob-
ability map, which was thresholded at 0.5 to predict the final ablation region.

evidence_fragments.content:
The simulation con-
sisted of three multiphysics steps [3,8]: electromagnetic field calculation using
the Helmholtz equation, tissue temperature estimation using the Pennes bio-
heat equation, and cellular necrosis estimation using the Arrhenius model. The
Helmholtz equation was solved using the finite element method (FEM), whereas
thePennesbioheatequationwassolvedusingthefinitedifferencemethod(FDM).
The vessel region was maintained at37◦C, with a convection boundary condition
applied at the vessel–tissue interface. Finally, the Arrhenius damage integral was
accumulated over time, and voxels with a final value greater than 1 were defined
as the necrotic region.

evidence_fragments.content:
The 60 patient CT datasets used for neural ablation prediction model training
and evaluation were divided into training, validation, and test sets with 36,
12, and 12 datasets, respectively. To reduce bias in the data distribution, the
datasets were sorted based on tumor size and the number of vessel voxels in the
vessel mask, and then evenly distributed across the three sets. The validation
set was used for early stopping with a patience of 5 to prevent overfitting during
training. Ablation zone prediction performance was evaluated using 1,000 cases
randomly sampled from the test set. The model achieved a Dice score of 95.06%
and an IoU of 90.78%, showing high agreement between the predicted ablation
zones and the numerical simulation results.

The clinical applicability of the proposed
planning method was evaluated by two MWA specialists using four categories:
optimal, acceptable, indeterminate, and not feasible. Plans rated as optimal or
acceptable were considered clinically applicable. As shown in Table 2, all antenna
insertion trajectories were rated as optimal or acceptable by both clinicians, in-
dicating clinically acceptable trajectory generation. In contrast, treatment dura-
tion and power settings showed greater inter-clinician variability, with one case
rated as indeterminate due to possible insufficient ablation, suggesting the need
for more quantitative criteria for treatment parameter selection.

legacy_cells.CK: Minimize target under-coverage plus weighted penalties for normal-tissue ablation, vertical deflection angle, and insertion length; enforce complete tumor coverage and avoid organs-at-risk collisions.

legacy_cells.DQ: 60 patient CT datasets; 813 tumor-centered volumes; 30,000 simulated input conditions; 1,000 test cases; 13 planning patients

legacy_cells.EA: Proposed plans achieved complete margin-included target coverage (CP 1.000); mean organ-damage rate was 0.175.
legacy_cells.EC: Compared with clinician-defined plans across 13 patients: mean AE 0.764 vs 0.495, CP 1.000 vs 0.998, OD 0.175 vs 0.389, and IPL 71.2 vs 73.6 mm.

legacy_cells.EM: Planning constraints include a 5 mm safety margin, complete tumor coverage, avoidance of organs-at-risk collisions, and penalties for normal-tissue ablation.
legacy_cells.FB: Voxel-space anatomy and treatment-response representation: patient-specific tumor/vessel masks are mapped to a final predicted ablation-region mask; no intermediate latent state is described.
legacy_cells.FL: Patient-specific tumor/vessel voxel masks are encoded by a 3D CNN; antenna pose, power, and duration generate affine modulation parameters in the decoder; the network predicts a terminal ablation mask; a genetic algorithm searches candidate plans using this fast forward model and anatomical constraints.
legacy_cells.FM: The authors propose patient-specific MWA planning using a neural ablation predictor as a fast forward model in a genetic algorithm, aiming to improve planning efficiency and quantitative treatment planning while considering anatomical constraints.
legacy_cells.FN: On 1,000 test cases, ablation prediction reached Dice 95.06% and IoU 90.78%. In 13 planning cases, mean AE was 0.764 vs 0.495, mean OD 0.175 vs 0.389, and mean IPL 71.2 vs 73.6 mm for clinician plans. Planning was about 420-fold faster than numerical simulation.
legacy_cells.FQ: The authors identify the high computational cost of multiphysics MWA simulation as a barrier to optimization-based planning requiring repeated forward evaluations.

limitations: Surrogate labels and compared plan outcomes come from simulations/the same learned surrogate, not observed ablation outcomes. Human CT geometry does not convert simulated lesion labels into clinical predictive validation.

Expert feasibility ratings are not evidence of improved patient outcomes, safety or actual treatment delivery.
